```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(fpp3)

dir <- tempfile(); dir.create(dir)
zipf <- file.path(dir, "bike.zip")
download.file("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/275/bike+sharing+dataset.zip",
              zipf, method = "curl", quiet = TRUE)
unzip(zipf, exdir = dir)

bike <- readr::read_csv(file.path(dir, "day.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(Date = as.Date(dteday),
            Rentals = cnt,
            Temp = temp * 41,          # the file stores these divided by their maximum
            Hum = hum * 100,
            Wind = windspeed * 67,
            Weather = weathersit,
            Holiday = holiday,
            Workday = workingday) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Date)

```


## Part 1: Make a plan

1. Plot `Rentals` and the weather variables. Describe the trend, the weekly pattern, the yearly seasonality, and any unusual days.
1. Before fitting anything, answer the following in a few sentences each. 
   * **What is known at forecast time?** At the end of day $t$, which values of `Rentals` and of the weather are available for forecasting day $t+3$? Which calendar information about day $t+3$ is known in advance?
   * **How will you score the forecasts?** RMSE, MAE, or a score aimed at the operations goal (for example, error on high-demand days only, or a heavier penalty for under-forecasting than for over-forecasting). Justify your choice.
   * **What validation period and training window will you use** to choose model settings? Justify the length and timing of your validation block(s), and your choice of an expanding or rolling window.
   * **What counts as a good forecast?** Choose one or more benchmark forecasts that use only information available three days ahead. Say how much better than the benchmark a model must be to be worth using.

Bike Rentals:
Low in the winter, then high in the summer (peaking around July).  Also, 2012 peaks much higher in the summer than 2011.  This is only two years worth of data, so I don't know if trend is the right word, but it seems like increasing trend (higher in 2012 than 2011), with the seasonal effect (higher in the summer, like linear + sinusoidal).  Moreover, since winters still stay near 0, you get increasing variance (like the air passengers) and might want to do a log.

**What is known at forecast time?**

At the end of day $t$, I think Rentals data is known immediately (as I understand it, you tap credit card on the bikes, everything is digital/immediate/in one system).  So there is no reporting lag.  You know the Rentals data up through day $t$.  You know the calendar information (Date, Workday, Holiday) out to $t+3$ (and beyond).

For weather, my very quick google AI answer says: "Weather forecasts for specific daily details—such as exact temperatures, wind speeds and directions, and humidity—are reliable out to 5 to 7 days."  And: "1 to 3 Days: High reliability (up to 90%–95% accuracy). Specific details like high/low temperatures, exact wind direction, and relative humidity changes are dependable."  So... I guess while the weather isn't exactly known, an available forecasted predictor variable can be used for the weather variables.

But in this data set we don't have the before-it-was-known weather forecasts.  So. I either use genuine temperature only up to day $t$ to forecast day $t+3$.  (Or maybe I could weirdly introduce some sort of synthetic temperature variable to mimic a 90-95% accurate temperature variable for days $t+1$, $t+2$, $t+3$. Which... nope.  but seems like an interesting idea.)

So, in the model, I guess I'm going to just say I only have temperature data through day $t$, but if weather prediction really is that accurate, I do wonder how bad the assumption is that I could actually use weather data out to $t+3$.  (Maybe prediction was less accurate in 2011.)

[ok... I now see that is covered later...]

**How will you score the forecasts?**

Some scattered thoughts: Perhaps having an extra bike or two available on peak days that then sits idle most of the year, it might be fine to "miss out on the sale" on the peak day.  (Actually: Do they sit idle? They must pack up bikes and store them.  There's no way they have the full fleet out even in the winter?  Or maybe they do.  I know Buffalo packs all of them up entirely for the winter; DC probably has a reduced fleet in the winter.)  On the other hand, if a bike is not available to a commuter when they want it, they may decide that commuting by bike is unreliable and that person may be lost as a potential daily bike commuter.  Now that I think about it, I'm not quite sure the use case for wanting to predict a daily number (as opposed to an overall seasonal max, say). It's not like a bunch of bikes get packed up each night and put back out in the morning.  Although I suppose you can decide which days you might grab a bunch of bikes for maintenance?  For that matter... I suppose we don't really know the size of the fleet. So perhaps some of these data points represent days when all the bikes were in use. So the data point represents the size of the fleet available at the time, instead of the actual demand.

(Also, if there are too many bikes out, relative to the number of docking stations, that can also suck.  I rode several miles out of my way to finally find a docking station with an open parking spot in Boston once.)

Ok all of which is to say, I don't know if there is a particular reason to highly penalize an undercount or an overcount. So, ... RMSE I guess?  I don't have an argument for anything else.


**What validation period and training window will you use**

Oof.  There's only two years of data with strong looking seasonality... This doesn't feel like enough data. Knee jerk reaction: I should use an expanding window. So at any given hypothetical point, use all the data that was available at that point. ON THE OTHER HAND: I do wonder about the bikes catching on with commuters.  Google says that bike sharing came to DC in 2008, but the "larger current regional network" launched in September 2010.  So it seems at least plausible that in 2011, bikesharing wasn't big with commuters and in 2012 maybe it was.  (So throwing out "old" data might be good).  In any case, I'm going to use an expanding window. But I wonder if that is actually the right move.

For a validation window, idk. 3 months.  Seems... medium.

So:

Train: 01/11 - 12/11; Validate 01/12 - 03/12

Train: 01/11 - 03/12; Validate 04/12 - 06/12

Train: 01/11 - 06/12; Validate 07/12 - 09/12

Train: 01/11 - 09/12; Test 10/12 - 12/12 (this is bad; only testing on some fall months?)

WELL! That's what I'm going to do.  But I think testing on October through December will be kind of bad.


**What counts as a good forecast?**

Benchmark forecasts: same day last week. (Temperature should be roughly the same; whatever weekly pattern exists should still be there; eg if commuter adoption changes over time, it shouldn't matter much in a week).  Also: rolling 7-day average.  (Same idea: temperature should be roughly the same; crazy weather events will be a bit smoothed out.)

I'm actually guessing that those benchmarks will be "pretty good." (whatever that means). So, completely arbitrarily, I will say a forecast is good if it is 5% better than those benchmarks.

More concretely: I will say a forecast is good if the RMSE if 5% lower than the same-day-last-week benchmark forecast.


## Part 2: Build the feature table

1. Build a table with one row per day and `Rentals` as the target. Include lags of the target, at least one rolling statistic of the target, calendar features, and weather features.
1. For each feature, state which day's data it uses and why it is known three days ahead.
1. Make the train/test split, report both sample sizes, and compute your benchmark forecasts on the validation and test periods.

```{r}

library(lubridate)

bike_model <- bike %>%
  arrange(Date) %>%
  mutate(
    # Rental history
    Rentals_lag3  = lag(Rentals, 3),  #will be most recently known
    Rentals_lag7  = lag(Rentals, 7),  #same day of the week

    # Seven-day rolling average, ending at t
    Rentals_avg7 = lag(
      zoo::rollmean(Rentals, k = 7,
                    fill = NA, align = "right"), #as I understand it, this is avg of t-9 thru t-3
      3
    ),

    # Observed weather, available through t (only using most recent for predict)
    Temp_lag3 = lag(Temp, 3),

    # Calendar information for the forecast date
    Day_of_week = wday(Date, label = TRUE),
    Month = month(Date)
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

```




```{r}

folds <- tibble(
  fold = 1:3,

  train_start = as.Date(c(
    "2011-01-01",
    "2011-01-01",
    "2011-01-01"
  )),

  train_end = as.Date(c(
    "2011-12-31",
    "2012-03-31",
    "2012-06-30"
  )),

  valid_start = as.Date(c(
    "2012-01-01",
    "2012-04-01",
    "2012-07-01"
  )),

  valid_end = as.Date(c(
    "2012-03-31",
    "2012-06-30",
    "2012-09-30"
  ))
)

folds

```


```{r}
test_data <- bike_model %>%
  filter(
    Date >= as.Date("2012-10-01"),
    Date <= as.Date("2012-12-31")
  )


validation_sets <- lapply(1:3, function(i) {

  train <- bike_model %>%
    filter(
      Date >= folds$train_start[i],
      Date <= folds$train_end[i]
    )

  valid <- bike_model %>%
    filter(
      Date >= folds$valid_start[i],
      Date <= folds$valid_end[i]
    )

  list(
    train = train,
    valid = valid
  )
})


# Fold 1
train1 <- validation_sets[[1]]$train
valid1 <- validation_sets[[1]]$valid

# Fold 2
train2 <- validation_sets[[2]]$train
valid2 <- validation_sets[[2]]$valid

# Fold 3
train3 <- validation_sets[[3]]$train
valid3 <- validation_sets[[3]]$valid

for (i in 1:3) {

  cat("\nFold", i, "\n")

  cat("Training:",
      nrow(validation_sets[[i]]$train), "\n")

  cat("Validation:",
      nrow(validation_sets[[i]]$valid), "\n")
}

cat("\nTest:", nrow(test_data), "\n")

```



```{r}

model_formula <- Rentals ~
  Rentals_lag3 +
  Rentals_lag7 +
  Rentals_avg7 +
  Temp_lag3 +
  Day_of_week +
  Month +
  Workday +
  Holiday

rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
}

###################################


validation_results <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:3) {

  train <- validation_sets[[i]]$train
  valid <- validation_sets[[i]]$valid

  # Fit model
  model <- lm(model_formula, data = train)

  # Predict
  predictions <- predict(model, newdata = valid)

  # Calculate RMSE
  fold_rmse <- rmse(valid$Rentals, predictions)

  # Save results
  validation_results <- rbind(
    validation_results,
    data.frame(
      Fold = i,
      Training_n = nrow(train),
      Validation_n = nrow(valid),
      RMSE = fold_rmse
    )
  )
}

validation_results

###################################

validation_predictions <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:3) {

  train <- validation_sets[[i]]$train
  valid <- validation_sets[[i]]$valid

  model <- lm(model_formula, data = train)

  predictions <- predict(model, newdata = valid)

  validation_predictions <- rbind(
    validation_predictions,
    data.frame(
      Date = valid$Date,
      Actual = valid$Rentals,
      Predicted = predictions,
      Fold = i
    )
  )
}

overall_validation_rmse <- rmse(
  validation_predictions$Actual,
  validation_predictions$Predicted
)

overall_validation_rmse


###################################


final_train <- bike_model %>%
  filter(Date < as.Date("2012-10-01"))

final_model <- lm(
  model_formula,
  data = final_train
)

test_predictions <- predict(
  final_model,
  newdata = test_data
)

test_rmse <- rmse(
  test_data$Rentals,
  test_predictions
)

test_rmse
```

Comparison to benchmarks:

```{r}

rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2, na.rm = TRUE))
}


bike_model %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  filter(Date >= "2012-01-01", Date <= "2012-12-31") %>%
  mutate(
    fold = case_when(
      Date <= "2012-03-31" ~ 1,
      Date <= "2012-06-30" ~ 2,
      Date <= "2012-09-30" ~ 3,
      TRUE ~ 4
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(fold) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    RMSE_last_week = rmse(Rentals, Rentals_lag7),
    RMSE_avg7 = rmse(Rentals, Rentals_avg7)
  )

```


I said beforehand that I'd compare to the last week's number.  I probably should have said I'd compare it to min(last week, rolling average).  In any case, the model was, for the most part, about the same as the rolling average.  Both were better than just taking last week's number.  And it seems like July-Aug is the easiest time period to predict.  TECHNICALLY, I guess the model did beat same-day-last-week, on all folds (and the testing), by at least 5%. But I'm moving the goal posts and it isn't very impressive when stacked against the rolling average.


## Part 3: Random forest
1. Fit a random forest with `ranger` using the default settings.
1. Fit at least one other setting, changing at least one of `mtry`, `min.node.size`, `max.depth` or `num.trees`. Choose between your settings on your validation period, using your score from Part 1. Show the comparison in a table.
1. Refit the chosen setting on all of the training data and score it on the test period. Also report its out-of-bag (OOB) error. Is it close to your validation error? Explain why or why not.
1. Make a permutation importance plot. Which features matter most?



```{r}

library(ranger)

set.seed(123)


rf_model <- ranger(
  formula = model_formula,
  data = bike_model %>%
    filter(Date <= "2011-12-31")
)

rf_model
```

ok. I think I'd like to mess with mty.  I think it should be pretty small, since Rentals_lag3, Rentals_lag7, Rentals_avg7 seem like they might be pretty similar.  (So basically, trying to avoid all of them, sometimes, via a small mty, seems like it might introduce some better tree-combos)

```{r}

library(purrr)

mtry_values <- 1:8

mtry_results <- map_dfr(mtry_values, function(m) {
  fold_preds <- map_dfr(seq_along(validation_sets), function(i) {
    train_df <- validation_sets[[i]]$train
    valid_df <- validation_sets[[i]]$valid

    fit <- ranger(
      formula = model_formula,
      data = train_df,
      mtry = m,
      num.trees = 500,
      seed = 246 + i
    )

    tibble(
      fold = i,
      Actual = valid_df$Rentals,
      Predicted = predict(fit, data = valid_df)$predictions
    )
  })

  # Overall RMSE across all validation rows (Folds 1–3)
  overall_val_rmse <- rmse(fold_preds$Actual, fold_preds$Predicted)

  tibble(
    mtry = m,
    Overall_Val_RMSE = overall_val_rmse
  )
})

knitr::kable(
  mtry_results,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Validation RMSE by mtry across Folds 1–3"
)

best_mtry <- mtry_results |>
  slice_min(Overall_Val_RMSE, n = 1) |>
  pull(mtry)

best_mtry


```


The best mtry came out as 7, which, ... not what I expected.  It's only a little better than the default.




```{r}

# 1. Refit on all training data prior to the test period (2011-01-01 through 2012-09-30)
final_train <- bike_model |>
  filter(Date < as.Date("2012-10-01"))

final_rf <- ranger(
  formula = model_formula,
  data = final_train,
  mtry = best_mtry,
  num.trees = 500,
  importance = "permutation",
  seed = 456
)

# 2. Out-of-bag (OOB) RMSE vs. Test RMSE
# ranger reports prediction.error as MSE for regression
oob_rmse <- sqrt(final_rf$prediction.error)

test_preds_rf <- predict(final_rf, data = test_data)$predictions
test_rmse_rf <- rmse(test_data$Rentals, test_preds_rf)

tibble(
  Metric = c("OOB RMSE (Final Train: Jan 2011 - Sep 2012)", "Test RMSE (Oct 2012 - Dec 2012)"),
  RMSE = c(oob_rmse, test_rmse_rf)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Out-of-Bag vs. Test Set RMSE")

# 3. Permutation variable importance plot
imp_df <- enframe(final_rf$variable.importance, name = "Feature", value = "Importance") |>
  arrange(Importance) |>
  mutate(Feature = factor(Feature, levels = Feature))

ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = Feature, y = Importance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Permutation Variable Importance (Final Random Forest)",
    subtitle = paste0("mtry = ", best_mtry, ", 500 trees"),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Increase in MSE When Permuted"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


```


7-day rolling average rentals (t-9 thru t-3) ended up being the most important variable (as determined by permutation).  (So it makes sense that that benchmark wound up being pretty good).

```{r}

etas <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2)
max_rounds <- 400

all_logs <- list()

for (e in etas) {
  fold_logs <- list()

  for (i in 1:3) {
    tr <- validation_sets[[i]]$train
    va <- validation_sets[[i]]$valid

    dtr <- xgb.DMatrix(
      as.matrix(mutate(tr[, xs_xgb], Day_of_week = as.numeric(Day_of_week))),
      label = tr$Rentals
    )
    dva <- xgb.DMatrix(
      as.matrix(mutate(va[, xs_xgb], Day_of_week = as.numeric(Day_of_week))),
      label = va$Rentals
    )

    curve_fit <- xgb.train(
      params = list(
        objective = "reg:squarederror",
        eta = e,
        max_depth = 3,
        subsample = 0.8,
        colsample_bytree = 0.8,
        seed = 123 + i
      ),
      data = dtr,
      nrounds = max_rounds,
      evals = list(train = dtr, valid = dva),
      verbose = 0
    )

    fold_logs[[i]] <- as_tibble(attributes(curve_fit)$evaluation_log) |>
      mutate(eta = factor(e), fold = i, n_tr = nrow(tr), n_va = nrow(va))
  }

  # Pool squared error across Folds 1-3 at each boosting round (iter)
  all_logs[[as.character(e)]] <- bind_rows(fold_logs) |>
    group_by(eta, iter) |>
    summarise(
      train_rmse = sqrt(weighted.mean(train_rmse^2, w = n_tr)),
      valid_rmse = sqrt(weighted.mean(valid_rmse^2, w = n_va)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

curves_df <- bind_rows(all_logs)

# 1. Table: chosen rounds and validation RMSE for each eta
xgb_summary_table <- curves_df |>
  group_by(eta) |>
  slice_min(valid_rmse, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(max_depth = 3, subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8) |>
  select(eta, max_depth, subsample, colsample_bytree,
         chosen_rounds = iter, validation_rmse = valid_rmse)

xgb_summary_table

# 2. Professor-style learning curve plot (train vs. valid across boosting rounds)
p_curve <- curves_df |>
  pivot_longer(c(train_rmse, valid_rmse), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(iter, rmse, colour = set)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ eta, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Boosting rounds", y = "RMSE", colour = NULL)

p_curve



```


The validation curves for each of the following:


eta is .02 -> global min around 150 or 200;

eta is .05 -> global min is around 75;

eta is .1 -> global min is around 50;

eta is .2 -> global min is around n=20, 


In all cases, the global min corresponds to *roughly* rmse of 1500; none of the eta's looks super good or bad (relative to one another).  I'm not sure how I should think about this.

Technically eta=.02 wound up with the smallest global min (among these four choices), for the valid_rmse curve (rmse of 1469).  But it doesn't look that substantially different from the other choices of eta.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

bike_model <- bike %>%
  arrange(Date) %>%
  mutate(
    # Rental history known at end of day t (for forecasting t+3)
    Rentals_lag3  = lag(Rentals, 3),
    Rentals_lag7  = lag(Rentals, 7),

    # Seven-day rolling average ending at t (lagged by 3 days -> t-9 through t-3)
    Rentals_avg7 = lag(
      zoo::rollmean(Rentals, k = 7, fill = NA, align = "right"),
      3
    ),

    # Observed weather available through day t
    Temp_lag3 = lag(Temp, 3),

    # Calendar features for forecast date t+3
    Day_of_week = wday(Date, label = TRUE),
    Month = month(Date)
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

folds <- tibble(
  fold = 1:3,
  train_start = as.Date(c("2011-01-01", "2011-01-01", "2011-01-01")),
  train_end   = as.Date(c("2011-12-31", "2012-03-31", "2012-06-30")),
  valid_start = as.Date(c("2012-01-01", "2012-04-01", "2012-07-01")),
  valid_end   = as.Date(c("2012-03-31", "2012-06-30", "2012-09-30"))
)

test_data <- bike_model %>%
  filter(
    Date >= as.Date("2012-10-01"),
    Date <= as.Date("2012-12-31")
  )

validation_sets <- lapply(1:3, function(i) {
  list(
    train = bike_model %>% filter(Date >= folds$train_start[i], Date <= folds$train_end[i]),
    valid = bike_model %>% filter(Date >= folds$valid_start[i], Date <= folds$valid_end[i])
  )
})

train1 <- validation_sets[[1]]$train
valid1 <- validation_sets[[1]]$valid
train2 <- validation_sets[[2]]$train
valid2 <- validation_sets[[2]]$valid
train3 <- validation_sets[[3]]$train
valid3 <- validation_sets[[3]]$valid

model_formula <- Rentals ~
  Rentals_lag3 +
  Rentals_lag7 +
  Rentals_avg7 +
  Temp_lag3 +
  Day_of_week +
  Month +
  Workday +
  Holiday

rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2, na.rm = TRUE))
}

mae <- function(actual, predicted) {
  mean(abs(actual - predicted), na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Store every benchmark and model's test predictions in one place
test_preds <- list(
  "7-day moving average (main benchmark)" = test_data$Rentals_avg7,
  "Same day last week (Rentals_lag7)"     = test_data$Rentals_lag7
)

# Expanding-window validation for lm
validation_results <- map_dfr(1:3, function(i) {
  fit_i <- lm(model_formula, data = validation_sets[[i]]$train)
  preds_i <- predict(fit_i, newdata = validation_sets[[i]]$valid)

  tibble(
    Fold = i,
    Training_n = nrow(validation_sets[[i]]$train),
    Validation_n = nrow(validation_sets[[i]]$valid),
    RMSE = rmse(validation_sets[[i]]$valid$Rentals, preds_i),
    MAE  = mae(validation_sets[[i]]$valid$Rentals, preds_i)
  )
})

validation_results

test_mae  <- mae(test_data$Rentals, test_predictions)

c(RMSE = test_rmse, MAE = test_mae)
```
